specPoints.text: describe how to carry out an acid-alkali titration

primer.text: From Acids, Alkalis & Titrations you know that acids supply hydrogen ions and alkalis supply hydroxide ions. A titration puts that chemistry to work: measured volumes are run together until neutralisation is complete, and the readings reveal how much of each is needed. This note walks through the apparatus, the method and the handling of results.

lessons.title: What is a titration?
lessons.opening: A titration is a method of analysing the concentration of solutions, most importantly in acid-base work. Running one solution from a burette into another, with an indicator watching, tells you exactly how much alkali neutralises a quantity of acid. Titrations also let you calculate moles, concentration or volume, and can be used to prepare salts.
keyPoints: Titrations analyse the concentration of solutions.
Acid-base titrations find exactly how much alkali neutralises a quantity of acid.
You may be asked for the moles, the concentration or the volume needed.
Salt preparation is another use, with the neutralisation done under controlled volumes.
The apparatus centres on a burette, a pipette and a conical flask.

low.restatement: A titration measures how much of one solution exactly reacts with another. The burette delivers measured volumes, the pipette fixes a starting amount, and the indicator shows when neutralisation is done.
low.analogy: It is like filling a glass from a tap until a float inside just lifts: the tap reading tells you exactly what was needed.
low.examPointer: Know what each piece of apparatus contributes: pipette for the fixed volume, burette for the variable one, flask for the reaction.

medium.restatement: Acid-base titrations answer quantitative questions: how much alkali neutralises a measured quantity of acid, and by extension the moles, concentration or volume behind that result. The method pairs a fixed pipetted volume with a variable burette volume, an indicator marks the endpoint, and repeated runs with concordant results make the answer trustworthy.
medium.analogy: Think of a set of scales: one pan holds a fixed, known mass, and you add measured amounts to the other pan until the beam exactly balances.
medium.examPointer: Why-questions reward purpose: state that titrations quantify neutralisation, then link concordant repeats to confidence in the answer.

check.stem: What is the main purpose of an acid-base titration?

options.text: To find how much alkali exactly neutralises a measured quantity of acid
options.explanation: Quantifying the neutralisation is the core purpose, and from it follow moles, concentrations and volumes.

options.text: To make the acid and alkali stronger
options.explanation: Nothing is concentrated by titrating; the method measures how much reacts.

options.text: To heat the solutions gently
options.explanation: No heating is involved in a titration at all.

options.text: To check the colour of the solutions
options.explanation: Colour is only watched through the indicator; the purpose is the measurement.

check.stem: Which piece of apparatus delivers the variable volume during a titration?

options.text: The burette
options.explanation: The burette is filled with acid and run in gradually, giving the variable volume that is recorded before and after.

options.text: The pipette
options.explanation: The pipette delivers one fixed volume, 25 cm3 of alkali here, into the flask.

options.text: The conical flask
options.explanation: The flask holds the reaction mixture; it measures nothing.
options.misconception: container mistaken for a measuring tool

options.text: The white tile
options.explanation: The tile only improves visibility of the colour change.
options.misconception: supporting item given a measuring role

check.stem: What is the pipette used for in this titration?

options.text: Placing exactly 25 cm3 of sodium hydroxide solution into the conical flask
options.explanation: The pipette and filler deliver one precise, fixed volume to start the titration.

options.text: Adding the indicator drop by drop
options.explanation: Indicator drops are added straight from a bottle; the pipette handles the alkali volume.

options.text: Measuring the gas released
options.explanation: No gas is measured in an acid-alkali titration.

options.text: Stirring the mixture during the titration
options.explanation: Swirling the flask does the mixing; the pipette is for measuring.

check.stem: Besides quantifying neutralisation, what can titrations be used to prepare?

options.text: Salts, made under carefully controlled reacting volumes
options.explanation: The note lists salt preparation as another use of titrations.

options.text: New elements
options.explanation: Titrations rearrange ions in solution; they never create elements.

options.text: Pure metals by electrolysis
options.explanation: Electrolysis is a separate process; titration is a volumetric method.

options.text: Indicators from plants
options.explanation: Indicators are extracted from plants directly; titrations consume them, not make them.

check.stem: Which quantities can a titration result help you calculate?

options.text: Moles, concentration and volume
options.explanation: These are exactly the quantities the note says may be asked for.

options.text: Mass of the apparatus only
options.explanation: Weighing apparatus is irrelevant to titration calculations.

options.text: Temperature change of the mixture
options.explanation: That belongs to calorimetry, not titration.

options.text: Colour intensity only
options.explanation: Colour is qualitative; the calculation targets are the three listed quantities.

lessons.title: How to carry out a titration
sourceHeadings: How to carry out a titration
lessons.opening: Good technique is a chain of small disciplines: flush the burette's jet space clear of bubbles, record readings to the nearest 0.05 cm3 at eye level, and set the flask on a white tile so the colour change shows. A rough titration finds the endpoint, then careful repeats add acid drop by drop until two results agree within 0.1 cm3.
keyPoints: Run some acid through first to remove air bubbles from the jet space.
Read the burette at eye level, to the nearest 0.05 cm3.
The white tile makes the colour changes more obvious.
Near the endpoint, add the acid one drop at a time.
Repeat until two results within 0.1 cm3 of each other are achieved.

low.restatement: First a rough run finds the endpoint quickly; then careful repeats drop by drop give precise volumes. Two results agreeing within 0.1 cm3 are called concordant, and their mean is the answer.
low.analogy: It is like parking in a tight space: the first attempt is quick and rough, then small corrections bring you perfectly into line.
low.examPointer: Technique marks come from the details: jet-space bubbles, eye-level meniscus readings, white tile, dropwise approach and the funnel removed.

medium.restatement: The disciplined sequence matters: flush the jet space, record both readings to 0.05 cm3, swirl during the rough run, then approach the endpoint dropwise on repeats until two concordant titres within 0.1 cm3 are achieved. The mean of the concordant pair, with the rough discarded, is the reported result, and the funnel must be out before you start.
medium.analogy: Treat the rough run as a rehearsal and the repeats as the performance: the rehearsal finds the cues, and the performance executes them precisely.
medium.examPointer: Explain questions contrast the rough with the repeats: rough for speed, dropwise repeats for accuracy, concordance as the quality gate.

check.stem: Why is a little acid run through the burette before you start?

options.text: To remove air bubbles, which collect in the jet space below the tap
options.explanation: A bubble in the jet space would later escape and falsify the volume delivered, so it is flushed out first.

options.text: To warm the burette to room temperature
options.explanation: Temperature plays no part; the flush targets bubbles.

options.text: To clean the burette of all acid traces
options.explanation: The burette is already filled with that acid; the small run clears the jet space specifically.

options.text: To check the tap still turns
options.explanation: A tap check is sensible but is not the stated purpose; bubbles are.

check.stem: To what precision should burette readings be recorded?

options.text: To the nearest 0.05 cm3
options.explanation: Both the starting point and the final titre are recorded to 0.05 cm3.

options.text: To the nearest whole cm3
options.explanation: Whole cm3 would waste the burette's precision and spoil the concordance test.

options.text: To the nearest 5 cm3
options.explanation: That is far too coarse for titration work.

options.text: Precision does not matter if the colour change is sharp
options.explanation: A sharp endpoint still needs precisely recorded volumes to be useful.

check.stem: What is the white tile under the conical flask for?

options.text: It makes the indicator's colour changes more obvious
options.explanation: Against a white background the endpoint colour flip is far easier to see.

options.text: It keeps the flask warm
options.explanation: No warming is wanted; the tile is about visibility.

options.text: It stops the flask from tipping over
options.explanation: Stability is incidental; the stated purpose is seeing the colour change.

options.text: It absorbs any spilled acid
options.explanation: Spill control is not the tile's stated job.

check.stem: Two titres of 14.90 cm3 and 15.00 cm3 are obtained. What can be said about them?

options.text: They are concordant, because they lie within 0.1 cm3 of each other
options.explanation: The difference is exactly 0.1 cm3, meeting the concordance rule, so both results count.

options.text: They are discordant and both must be discarded
options.explanation: Results within 0.1 cm3 are concordant and are kept, not discarded.

options.text: Only the larger value may be used
options.explanation: Concordant results are averaged, not cherry-picked.

options.text: The rough titre should be included in the mean
options.explanation: The rough run is always left out; the mean uses the concordant pair.

check.stem: Why must the funnel be removed from the burette before titrating?

options.text: Drips from the funnel would fall into the burette and falsify the initial reading
options.explanation: A late drip adds volume you never recorded, which corrupts the titre.

options.text: The funnel would react with the acid
options.explanation: Funnels are inert in this context; the problem is stray drips, not reaction.

options.text: The funnel blocks the jet space
options.explanation: The jet space is below the tap; the funnel sits at the top.

options.text: It is only a matter of tidiness
options.explanation: Tidiness is not the issue; measurement integrity is.

glossary.definition: A method in which one solution is run into another until neutralisation is just complete.
The amount of dissolved substance in a given volume of solution.
The long graduated tube with a tap that delivers the variable, recorded volume.
The device that transfers one fixed volume, here 25 cm3, into the flask.
The volume delivered by the burette between the starting and final readings.
Describes two results lying within 0.1 cm3 of each other, so both are trusted.
The reaction in which an acid and an alkali react completely, leaving the indicator's endpoint passed.
The moment the indicator changes colour sharply, showing neutralisation is complete.

workedExample.prompt: A titration gives a rough titre of 15.50 cm³ and two further titres of 14.90 cm³ and 15.00 cm³. Calculate the mean titre using the concordant results.
steps: The rough titre is discarded, leaving the two concordant results: 14.90 cm³ and 15.00 cm³.
The two results agree within 0.1 cm³, so they are concordant and both are used.
